opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think verification is actually one of the places where AI is going to change mathematics the most, and maybe sooner than people expect.

Right now, verifying a proof is a very human, very social process. You write a paper, you send it to a journal, and a referee, often a busy colleague, spends weeks or months going through it line by line. For a long, technical paper, honestly, a lot of the checking is done on trust. You trust the author's reputation, you check the key steps carefully, and you skim the routine estimates. Errors do slip through, and sometimes they're found years later.

I see AI helping in two different ways. The first is informal checking. Language models are getting good enough that you can hand them a draft and say, "Go through this lemma and tell me if anything is wrong." They're not perfect. They'll sometimes flag things that are fine, or miss subtle issues. But as a first pass, they catch a surprising number of sign errors, missing assumptions, and inequalities going the wrong way. In my own work on optimization, the proofs often involve long chains of algebraic manipulations, and having a tireless assistant that checks each step is genuinely useful.

The second, and I think more profound, change is the connection to formal verification, with systems like Lean. Formal proof has always had the promise of absolute certainty, but the cost of formalizing was enormous. You could spend months formalizing something a mathematician would write in five pages. If AI can do much of that translation from informal mathematics into a formal language, then the checking becomes mechanical and completely reliable. The human then only needs to verify that the formal statement actually says what we intended, which is a much smaller job.

That also changes the role of AI in discovery. When AI proposes a proof, the natural concern is, "Can I trust this?" And the answer is: you shouldn't trust it blindly, but you also don't have to. You verify it, either by careful human reading or, ideally, formally. When I worked with ChatGPT on an open problem, that's exactly how it went. The model would suggest ideas, many of them wrong, and my job was to be the verifier, filtering out the bad ones and recognizing the promising ones. Being able to check quickly is what makes the collaboration productive.

So I think we'll move toward a world where generating candidate arguments is cheap, and verification becomes the central skill and the central infrastructure. Mathematicians will spend less time grinding through routine steps and more time on judgment: which questions matter, which statements are the right ones to prove, and what the results actually mean.

r002.rationale: It says errors may be found years later, but does not describe a result accepted by the field whose proof later proves unsalvageable.

r003.rationale: It predicts AI will make checking quicker, saying fast verification will help make AI collaboration productive and become central infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think verification is actually the part of mathematics where AI will land first and hardest, and it's worth separating that from the more glamorous question of whether AI can discover new theorems.

Right now, when a paper comes in, a referee reads it. That referee is a busy human who is, frankly, often skimming. Mistakes slip through all the time. Most of them are minor, a missing hypothesis or a constant that's off, but occasionally something load-bearing is wrong and nobody notices for years. The system works mostly on trust and reputation, not on actual checking.

What's changing is that we now have two things coming together. One is formal proof assistants like Lean, where a proof is checked by a computer kernel and there's no ambiguity about whether it's correct. The other is language models that are getting quite good at translating informal mathematical arguments into that formal language. For a long time, formalization was so labor-intensive that only a handful of people did it, and only for a few flagship results. If AI can bring the cost of formalizing down by an order of magnitude or two, then it becomes realistic to say, "Every paper comes with a machine-checked certificate."

I don't think we're fully there yet. The models still struggle with long, messy, research-level arguments, and a lot of real mathematics lives in the gap between what's written down and what the author actually means. Filling in those gaps is exactly where the hard work is. But I've been genuinely surprised by how fast the frontier has moved in the last couple of years. Things I would have said were five years away are happening now.

The part I find most interesting is what this does to the culture. If verification becomes cheap, the question "is this correct?" gets settled by a machine, and the human conversation shifts to "is this interesting, is this the right way to think about it, does this explain anything?" That's actually the part of mathematics I care about most. So I don't see this as AI taking something away from mathematicians. I see it as removing a bottleneck that was never the point in the first place.

There's also a more subtle effect. When you know your argument will be checked line by line, you write differently. You're more honest with yourself about what you've actually proven. I think that discipline will make us better mathematicians, not worse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses formalizing and checking proofs, but does not mention researchers trying to extend a proof as part of verification.

r002.rationale: It says load-bearing mistakes can go unnoticed for years, but does not describe a result first accepted by the field and later found to have an unsalvageable proof.

r003.rationale: It predicts that AI will reduce the cost of formalization substantially, making machine-checked certificates realistic and verification cheap.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts computer checking with busy human referees, but does not state that AI has more patience than humans when verifying mathematics.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could make rigorous proof verification a much more practical part of doing mathematics. Usually, we write proofs in natural language, and we rely on other mathematicians to check that the reasoning is sound. That works remarkably well, but there can be gaps, and checking a long, complicated proof takes a lot of effort.

With a formal proof assistant, you can express the argument in a precise language and have a computer check each logical step. The challenge is that translating a mathematical proof into that language can itself be a huge amount of work. AI could help bridge that gap—taking an informal argument, proposing a formal version, and helping fill in the intermediate steps.

The crucial distinction is that the AI proposes the proof, but a separate proof checker verifies it. You don’t have to trust the AI’s confidence or how convincing its explanation sounds. You still need to make sure the formal statement captures the question you intended to ask, but you get a much stronger check on the argument itself.

That could also change how we develop proofs. Instead of verification happening only at the end, you could get feedback while you’re exploring an idea: this step follows, this one needs another assumption, this part is still missing.

r003.rationale: It says AI could make verification more practical and provide feedback, but does not clearly predict that AI will accelerate the verification process.

r004.rationale: It does not compare AI’s patience with humans’ when verifying mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could make rigorous proof verification a much more routine part of mathematics. There’s a distinction between an AI reading a proof and saying, “This looks right,” and a proof assistant checking every logical step. The first can be useful, but it can also miss a subtle error. The second gives us a much stronger form of assurance, provided the statement and assumptions have been formalized correctly.

The challenge is that translating a mathematical argument into that formal language takes substantial effort. AI could help bridge that gap: take a proof written in ordinary mathematical prose, fill in intermediate steps, and propose a formal version that a proof assistant can check. If a step fails, that becomes feedback for another attempt.

What excites me is the possibility of making that process accessible to working mathematicians. You could spend more time on the ideas while getting precise feedback about where an argument needs more justification. That could change both how we check finished proofs and how we develop them.
